text:
The passage rewards a reader who attends to what is missing from it. Sarah does not appear anywhere in the chapter, and the book announces her death in the verse which immediately follows; the scene implies, though it never states, that something in the household did not survive the mountain. Abraham returns to the servants, and of Isaac nothing is said. At exactly the moment where a lesser story would linger, the narrator turns away; and the silence is more than mere absence, being itself a form of testimony.

It may be objected that the chapter simply reflects the conventions of ancient narrative, which rarely reports what its characters feel and never explains; and in some sense this may perhaps be true. Restraint, however, is in this voice a kind of accusation, and the reticence of the chapter is deliberate. The narrator knows what he is doing, for elsewhere he reports feeling readily enough. Esau cries out; Jacob is afraid; Joseph weeps.
